title: Part Two, Chapter 7: The Summons from the Underworld

verses.t: And they went off very happily to play ball in the ball court, and it was very far where they went to play by themselves; and they swept and cleaned the ball court of their fathers. And when the lords of the underworld heard this, they said, "Who are these who have begun to play over us again, and have no respect for us, making all this noise? Did not that Hun-hun-ahpu and Vucub-hun-ahpu die, who wanted to make themselves great in our presence? Let someone go and call them at once!" said Hun-came and Vucub-came again, and all the lords. And they called them, and said to their messengers, "Go, tell them to come here, for the lords say so, and they shall play with us; seven days from now let them be here, and we shall play," it was said to the messengers. And then they came by a broad road, one of the many, which went straight to their house, and they came straight to the old woman. And she was washing when the messengers of the underworld arrived, and they said, "The lords say that the boys are to come to the underworld, and they give them a term of seven days, within which they will be waiting for them." This was said to Xmucane. "Very well," she said. "They will go there; they will go there, lord messengers." And the messengers went away and returned, and the old woman was troubled: "How shall I send to call my grandsons? What shall I say about their summons? Truly, the messengers came just like this long ago, when they came for their fathers," said the old woman; and very sorrowfully she went into her house by herself. And then a louse dropped down, and the old woman caught it and put it on her hand, and the louse wriggled and walked about. And she said to it, "You, my grandson, would you like me to send you to call my grandsons at the ball court?" it was said to the louse. "Go and tell them that their grandmother says the messengers of the underworld have come to her to call them, and that seven days from now they must go; tell them that their grandmother says so," it was said to the louse. And then the louse went off wriggling. And a boy called Tamazul, who was a toad, was sitting on the road, and the toad said to the louse, "Where are you going?" And the louse said, "I am going to the young men, the boys, and I carry the message in my belly." "Very well," said the toad, "but I see that you cannot run. Do you want me to swallow you? Then you will get there. Look how I run, and so we shall soon arrive." "Very well," said the louse to the toad, and then the toad swallowed the louse. And the toad went running, and when he was tired and no longer running, he met a great snake called Zaquicaz, who said to him, "Where are you going, Tamazul, boy?" This was said to Tamazul by Zaquicaz. And the toad said to the snake, "I am a messenger; I carry the message in my belly." And the snake said, "I see that you are tired and cannot run, and you will not get there soon," said the snake to the toad. "Come here, I shall swallow you." And then the snake Zaquicaz swallowed the toad; and from then on the snake took this as its food, eating toads. The snake went running, when it was met by a bird called Vac; and then it came over the ball court; and from then on this bird took this as its sustenance, eating snakes in the forests. And when the Vac arrived, it perched on the parapet of the ball court, where Hun-ahpu and Xbalanque were enjoying themselves playing ball; and as the Vac arrived it sang, "Vacgo, vacgo" (that is, "here is the Vac"). And they said, "What song is this? Bring the blowguns!" And then, shooting the Vac with the blowgun, the pellet went straight and struck it in the pupil of the eye, and it fell, spinning; and then they caught it and asked it, "What have you come here for?" they said to the Vac. And it said, "Here in my belly I bring a message. First cure my eye, and then I shall tell it." "Very well," they said; and taking a little of the rubber of the ball, they put it on the Vac's eye, and it was called Cotzquic (that is, the rubber of a certain plant), because it at once cured the bird's eye, and it saw well after it was cured. And they said to it, "Come, say what you bring." And then it vomited up a great snake, and they said to the snake, "Come, say at once what you bring," it was said to the snake. And it said, "Very well," and then it vomited up the toad. And it was said to him, "What is your message? Say it at once." And he said, "Here in my belly I bring the message." And then he tried to vomit, and could not; his mouth only filled with something like slobber. He kept trying to vomit, and could not. And the boys wanted to beat him, and said to him, "You are a liar and a cheat," and they kicked him in the rump; and he tried again, and made nothing but slobber in his mouth. And then the boys opened his mouth and tore it, and searched in his mouth, and found the louse stuck to the toad's teeth, for it had stayed in his mouth and he had not swallowed it. And so he acts as if he vomits; and he was scorned and beaten, and he has no assigned food, nor was any assigned to him, and he does not run, but is food for snakes. "Come, speak," they said to the louse, and then it gave its message: "Your grandmother says, boys, young men: 'Go, call them, for messengers have come from the underworld, from Hun-came and Vucub-came, saying that they are to go there within seven days. Let them come here, they say, and we shall play ball; and let them come with the gear of the game: the rubber ball, the yoke, the bat and the leather. Let them go and entertain them, for the lords say so.' This is what your grandmother says, for the messenger of the lords came so, and so I have come to call you." "Yes, so it shall be," they said in their hearts on hearing the message. And at once they came and reached their grandmother, and went only to give their grandmother notice.

"We are going, lady, and we have only come to let you know. And we leave you this sign of our word: each of us will plant a cane in the middle of our house, and this will be the sign of our death. If it dries up, you will say, 'They have just died'; but if it sprouts, you will say that your grandsons are alive. Grandmother, and you, mother, do not weep, for the sign of our word remains with you." And when they went, Hun-ahpu planted one and Xbalanque planted another; and they planted them only in the house, and did not plant them in the fields, nor in moist earth, but in dry earth; in the middle of their house they left them planted.
